When the head reiss at sirii: above the brim of the pelvis, . and is not far advanced, the fontanel se may be plainly felt with the finger, commonly towards the side of the pelvis : this is the place where the coronal crosses the sagittal future, and. the bones are a little fepaiated

pace.c:
PACE, a measure taken from the space between the two feet of a man, in walking; usually reckoned two feet and a half, and in some men a yard or three feet.

The geometrical pace is five feet ; and 60000 such paces make one degree of the equator.

Pace, in the manege, is of three kinds, viz. walk, trot, and gallop ; to which may be added jn amble, because some horses have it naturally.

P A C

Horses winch go Ihuffting or mixed paces, between the walk and amble, are for the most part of no value ; which commonly proceeds from their fiery temper, and sometimes from a weakness in their reins or legs, PACHAMAC, a temple of Peru, in South America, dedicated by the Indians to the supreme being : it gives its name to the adjacent country. PACHODECARHOMBIS, in natural history, the name of a genus of fossils, of the class of the selenitae, expressing a thick rhomboidal body, ccmpofed often planes.

pacificocean.c:
PACIFIC OCEAN, that vast ocean which separates Asia from America : it is called Pacific, from the moderate weather the first mariners who failed in it met with between the tropics ; and it was ca’led south-sea, be rouse the Spaniards crofted' the isthmus of Darien from north to south, when they first discovered it: though it is properly the Western ocean, with regard toAmerica.

PiVCK, in commerce, denotes a quantity of goods, made up in loads, or bales, for carriage.

A pack of wool is seventeen stone and two pounds, or a horse’s load.

package.c:
PACKAGE, is a small duty of one penny in the pound, paid for all goods not particularly rated.

PACOS, in zoology. SeeCAMELUs.

pactolus.c: PACTOLUS, a river of Lydia in the lefTer Asia, celebrated by the ancient poets for its golden fands.

paddoc.c: PADDOC, or Paddoc-course, a piece of ground encompassed with pales or a wall, and taken out of a park for exhibiting races with grey-hounds, for plates, wagers, or the like.

paderborne.c: PADERBORNE, the capital of the bishopric of the same name in Westphalia : E. long. 8° 25', N.Iat. 51° 45'.

padstow.c: PADSTOW, a market town of Cornwall, thirty miles weft of Launcefton.

padua.c: PADUA, the capital of the Paduan, in Italy, a city of a circular form, situated twenty-two miles weft of Venice: E. long. 120 15'* N. Iat. 450 30'.

paduan.c:
PADUAN, a province of Italy, in the territories of Venice, thirty-five miles long, and almost as much in breadth ; bounded by the Trevifane on the north, by the duchy of Venice on the east, by the Polefin de Rovigo on the south, and by the Vicentin on the weft.

Paduan, among the medalists, a -modern medal struck in imitation of the antique ; or a new medal struck with all the marks and characters of antiquity.

PADUS, in botany. ^See Prunus.

PiEAN, among the ancient pagans, was a song of rejoicing sung in honour of Apollo, chiefly used on occasions of victory and triumph.

P^ean, in the ancient poetry, a foot confiding of four syllables ; of which there are four kinds, the paean primus, secun^us, &c.

The paean primus consists of one long syllable and three short ones, or a trochaeus and pyrrhichius, as temporibus ; the paean secundus consists of a short filia- « hie, a long, and two short, or an iambus and a pyrrhichius, as potentia ; the paean tertius consists of two short syllables, a long and a short one, or a pyrrhichius and a trochaeus, as animatus ; the paean quartus consists of. three short syllables and a long one, or a pyrrhichius and iambus, as celeri tas.

paederota.c:
PAEDEROTA, in botany, a genus of 'the diandria monogynia class, of which there are two species, none of them natives of Britain.

P ADO-bap tism> infant-baptism, or that conferred on children.

paconia.c:
PACONIA, in botany, a genus of the pofyandria digynia class. 'The calix consists of five leaves, and the corolla of five petals ; the stylus is wanting ; and the capsule contains many feeds. There are two species, none of them natives of Britain.

The root of this plant is a very celebrated medicine in nervous cafes.

pagan.c: PAGAN, a heathen, gentile, or idolater ; ore who adores false gods. See Mythology.

paganalia.c: PAGANALIA, certain festivals observed by the ancient Romans in the month of January. T hey were instituted by Servius Tullius, who appointed a certain number of villages (pagi), in each of which an altar was to be raised for annual sacrifices to their tutelar gods ; at which all *. the inhabitants were to assist, and give presents in money, according to their sex and age, by which means the number of country-people was known. The servants upon this occasion offered cakes to Ceres and Tellus, to obtain plentiful harvests.

paganellus.c: PAGANELLUS, in ichthyology. See Gobius. - PAGANISM, the religious worship and discipline of pagans ; or, the adoration of idols and false gods. See 1 Idolatry and Mythology.

pageant.c:
PAGEANT, a triumphal car, chariot, arch, or other like pompous decoration, variously adorned with colours, flags, &c. carried about in public shews, processions, <&c. PAGOD, or Pagoda, a name whereby the East-Indians call the temple in which they worship their gods.

Pagod, or Pagoda, is also the name of a gold and silver \ coin, current in feveral parts of the East-Indies.

Px^IN, is defined to be an uneasy sensation arising from a sudden and violent solution of the continuity, or some other accident in the nerves, membranes, vessels, muscles, <soc. of the body ; or, according to some, it consists in a motion of the organs of sense ; and, according to others, * it is an emotion of the soul occasioned by these organs.

painting.c:
PAINTING, the art of representing natural bodies, and giving them an appearance of life, by the turn of lines, and the degrees of colours.

Whoever would apply himself to painting, fays Leonardo da Vinci, must in the first place learn perspective : this will enable him to dispose things in their proper places, and to give the due dimensions to each : having done this, he must learn to design ; ch using for that purpose some able master, who at the same time may give him some insight into the colours of figures : he ought then to consult nature, to confirm himself in what he has already learnt ; and, laftly, let him apply himself to the study and imitation of the greatest masters, in order to get a habit of reducing* what he has learnt into practice.

To judge of the goodness of a painting, it is necessary to establish to ourselves a system of rules to be applied occasionally ; and to assist the judgment herein, the following rules have been laid down : 1. The subject must: be finely imagined, and, if possible, improved in the painter’s hands ; he must think well as an historian, poet* philosopher, or divine, and more especially as a painter, in making a wife use o,f all the advantages of his art, and in finding expedients to supply its defers. 2. The ex>- pression must be proper to the subject, and the characters of the persons : it must be strong, so that the dumb shew may be perfe&Jy and readily understood : every part of the picture must contribute to this end ; colours, animals, draperies, and especially the actions of the figures, and above all the airs of the heads. 3. There must be one principal light; and this, and all the subordinate ones, with the shadows and reposes, must make one entire and harmonious mafs ; the feveral parts must be well con- , aed ted and con trailed, so as so render the whole as grateMi

i -‘fal to the eye, as a good piece of musick to the ear. By this means the pi&ure is not only more delightful, but better seen and comprehended. 4. The drawing mud be just ; nothing mull be fiat, lame, or ill proportioned; and these proportions should vary according to the chara&ers of the persons drawn. The colouring, whether gay or solid, mud be natural, beautiful, and clean, and what the eye is delighted with, in shadows, as well as lights and middle tints ; &od whether the colours are laid on thick, or finely wrought, they mud appear to be done by a light and accurate hand. Laftly, Nature mud be the foundation that mud be seen at the bottom ; but nature mad 'be raised. and improved, not only from what is commonly seen, to what is but rarely met with, but even yet higher, from a judicious and beautiful idea in the painter’s mind, so that grace and greatness may shine throughout .more or lefs according to the fubjed.

Painting is of various kinds, according to the materials used, the matter upon which they are applied, and the manner of applying them ; as painting in oil, in watercolours, fresco,

'Pa i sting in oil. The whole secret of painting in oil consids i.n grinding the colours with nut oil, or linseed-oil ; but the manner of working is very different from that in frcfco, or in water, by reason the oil does not dry near so fad, which gives the painter an opportunity of touching and 're touching all the parts of his figures as often as he pleases ; which in the other methods of painting is a thing impracticable. The figures done in oil are also capable ■of more force and boldness ; insomuch that the black becomes blacker, when ground with oil, than with water; besides, all the colours mixing better together, makes the colouring the Tweeter, more delicate and agreeable, and gives an union and tenderness to the whole, inimitable in any of the other manners.

Painting in oil is performed on canvas, on walls, wood, stone, and all forts of metals. 1 . Painting on cloth or canvas is done as follows : The canvas being Aretched on a frame, •give it a layer of size, or paste-water, and then go over it with a pumice-done to smooth off the knots. By means of the size, the little threads and hairs are all laid close on the cloth, and the little holes filled^ip, so that no colour can pass through. When the cloth is dry, lay on oker in <jil, which may be mixed with white-lead to make it dry the sooner. When dry, go over it again with the pumice done, to make it smooth. After this a second couch is sometimes applied, composed of white-lead andalittlecharcoalblack, to render the ground of an assi colour. Others prime the canvas in the following manner: They first smooth the canvas with a pumice-done, size it over with a good size ,and a little honey, and let it stand to dry,; after which they lay it over with whiting and size, mixed with a little honey : the use of the honey is to prevent it from Cracking, peeling, and breaking out ; on this they first draw the picture with a coal, and then lay on the colours. 2. Painting qa walls; When the wad is dry, they give it two or three washes with boiling oil; till the plader remains rjuite greasy, and will imbibe no more; upon this they lay drying colours, fucji as white-chalk, red-oker, or other chalks beaten pretty Aiff.- When this couch or layer is well dried, the fubje<dor design is Sketched out, and afterwards painted over, mixing a little varnish with their flours* to save the varmlhing afterwards. la order the

better to fortify the wall again d mo i dure, forr.e cover it with a p! ier of lime, marble-dttft, or a cement made of beaten tiles fc.ked in linseed-oil ; and at lad prepare a competition of green pitch, madic, and thick vain ish boiled together, which they apply hot ever the former pbder ; and when dry, lay on the colours as before. Others, in fine, make their plader with lime-mortar, tile-cement, and fand; and this being dry, they apply another of ]im$, cement, andiron fcorke; which being well beaten, and incorporated with linseed-oil and whites of eggs, makes an excellent plader. When this is dry, the colours are laid on as before.. 3. In painting on wood, they usually give their ground a couch cr layer of white tempered with size, and then proceed as in painting on walls. 4. In painting on done or metals, it is not necessary to lay them ever with size, but only to add a slight couch of colours before the design is drawn on it; nor even is this done on (tone's, whose you would have she ground appear, as in certain marbles and agates of extraordinary colours.

All the colours used in fresco are. good in oil, except white of lime and marble dud. Those chiefly used aTe

. white-lead, or ceruse, yellow and white mad scot, orpiment, vermilion, lacca,.blue a,nd green ashes, verdigreafe, indigo, smalt, black-lead, ivory-black, lamp-black,

As to oils, the bed are* those of linseed, walnuts, spike, and turpentine. The drying oils are nut-oil, boiled with litharge and sandarach, and oiherwife with spirit of wine, madic, and gum-lacca.

In the preparation of oil-colours, care mud be taken that they be ground fine; that in putting them on a pallet, those which will not dry of themselves-be mixed with drying oil, or other ingredients of a dying quality; and that the tinged colours be mixed in as small quantities 2s possible. As to the situation of the colours, the pure stand strong ed mud ^ placed in the front of the piece, and the colouring varied according to the subjest, time, and pladg. If the subjest be .grave, melancholy, or terrible, the genera] tint of the colouring mud incline to brown and black, or red and gloomy ; but it mud be gay and pleas fant, in fubje&s of joy -and triumph.

palaestra.c:
PALAESTRA, in G r e ci a n ntiq ui t y ,* & public building, where the youth exercised themselves in wrest ling, running, playing ar quoits,

PALAlSTROPHYLAX, was the director of the palasdra and .the exererfes performed there.

*57. PALAIS, a town of France, in the province of Gascony, capital of the lower Navarre, situated in W. long. i° 8', N. lat. 43° 23'.

palamboang.c: PALAMBOANG, or Palambang, the capital of a kingdom at the ead end of the island of Java, in the EaA-In* dies, situated on the straits of Bassy, tive long, 114°, S. lat. 70 30',' and separated from the island of Bassy by a narrow Arair.

palamedia.c: PALAMEDIA, in ornithology, a genus belonging to the order of grail as. The bill is conical, the superior mandible being crooked; and the feet have three divided toes. There are two species, both natives of Brasil.

palaria.c:
PAL ARIA, arpong the Romans, a kind of exercise, performed at a dake by the soldiers. The dake being fixed in the ground and six feet high above it, the young undisciplined soldiers advanced against it, armed with a hurdle and cudgel, indeed of .a shield and sword, and went through all the rules of attack and defence, as if actually

engaged

engaged with an adversary. Sometimes they flood at a distance; and attacked withTniffive weapons, at the same time using all the requisite motions for defending themselves, and warding off what might be thrown against them.

palatinate.c: PALATINATE, a province, or' signiory, possessed by a palatine.

palatine.c:
PALATINE, or count palatine, a title anciently given to all persons who had any office or employment in the prince’s palace ; but afterwards conferred on those delegated by princes to hold courts of jufUce in the provinces ; and on such among the lords as hid a palace, that is, a court of justice, in their own houses.

At present the word palatine is restrained to a prince of Germany, or a lord of Poland, possessed of a palatine.

PALATO-salping^us. See Anatomy, p. 303.

Palato staphylinus, in anatomy. See Anatomy, p. 303.

pale.c:
PALE, a little pointed stake or piece of wood, used in making inclosures, reparations, he. The pale was an instrument of punishment and execution among the ancient Romans, and still continues so among the Turks. Hei>ce empaling, the passing a {harp pale up the fundament through the body.

Pale, in heraldry, one of the honourable ordinaries of an escutcheon ; being the representation of a pale or stake placed upright, and comprehending the whole height of the coat from the top of the chief to the point. When the pale is single, it is to contain one third of the breadth of the shield. See Plate CXXXIV. fig. 7.

palermo.c: PALERMO, the capital 'of the; island of Sicily, situated on the* north coast of that island, on a bay of the Mediterranean sea: in E. long. 130, N. lat. 38° 3c/.

palestine.c:
PALESTINE, a part of Asiatic Turky, situated between thirty-six and thirty-eight degrees of east longitude, and between thirty-one and thirty-four degrees of north latitude : it is bounded by Mount Libanus which divides it from Syria, on the north ; by Mount Hermon, which se* parates it from Arabia Deferta, on the east ; by the mountains of Seir and the Desarts of Arabia Petrsea, on the south ; and by the Mediterranean sea, on the weft.

It was called Palestine, from the Philistines who inhabited the seacoasts. It was also called Judea, from Judah ; and the Holy Land, from our Saviour’s residence and sufferings in it ; and it is called Canaan, and the Promised Land, in the scriptures.

It is 150 miles in length, and 80 in breadth ; and in the time of Solomon it seems to have extended from the Mediterranean sea to the river Euphrates.

palestrina.c: PALESTRINA, a city of Italy, in the pope’s territory and Campania of Rome, situated thirty miles east of Rome.

palimbam.c: PALIMBAM, a town on the island of Sumatra, in the East-Indies, situated in E. long. 1O30, S. lat 30.

paling.c:
PALING, a sort of fencing for fruit-trees planted in fields, wherein three smal! posts are creeled at a foot and a half distance one from another, and near the top nailed to each Other with cross-bars.

palingenesia.c:
PALINGENESIA, among divines, signifies the same with regeneration.

Among chemrfts, it denotes the producing a body from its principles.

palinody.c: PALINODY, a discourse contrary to a preceding one : hence the phrase palinodiam canere was taken for a recantation.

palisade.c:
PALISADE, in fortification, an inclosure of stakes or piles driven into the ground, each six or seven inches fquarei and eight feet long, three whereof are hid under ground.

PALISSE', in heraldry, a bearing like a range of palisades before a fortification, represented on .a fesse, rifing up a confiderable"height, and pointed a-top, with the field appearing between tfiem. See Plate CXXXIV. fig. 8.

PALIURUS, in botany. See Rhamnus.

pall.c: PALL, in heraldry, denotes a kind. of cross representing the pallium, or archiepiscopal ornament sent from Rome to the Metropolitans. See Plate CXXXIV. fig. 9.

palla.c: PALLA, in Roman antiquity, a mantle which women wore over the gown called stola. It was borne on the left {boulder; whence passing to the other side, under the right arm, the two ends were bound under the left arm, leaving the breast and arm quite bare,

palladium.c: PALLADIUM, in antiquity, a statue of the goddess Pal. las, supposed to have dropped down from heaven, pre* served in Troy, whereon the fate of that city is said to have depended.

pallet.c:
PALLET, among painters, a little oval table, or piece of wood, or ivory, very thin and smooth ; on and round which the painters place the feveral colours' they have occasion for, to be ready for the pencil. The middle ferves to mix the colours on, and to make the tints required in the work. It has no handle, bqt instead thereof, a hole at one end to put the thumb through to hold it.

Pallet, in heraldry, is nothing but a small pale, confiding of one half of it in breadth, and therefore there are sometimes feveral of them upon one shield.

Pallet* in (hip-building, is a room within the hold, closely parted from it, in which by laying some pigs of lead, he. a (hip may be sufficiently ballast ed, without losing room in the hold ; which, therefore, will serye for the flowing the more goods.

palliation.c: PALLIATION, or a palliative cure, in medicine, is when, in desperate and incurable diseases, after predicting the fatal event, the physician prescribes some remedies for mitigating the pain or some other urgent symptoms, as in ulcerated cancers, or cancerous fistulas, and the like.

pallium.c:
PALLIUM, or Pall, an archiepiscopal vestment, of white woollen cloth, about the breadth of a border, made - round, and thrown over the shoulders.

Palm. sun day, in the Christian church, the Sunday next before Ealler ; being so called in memory of our Saviour’s triumphal entry into Jerusalem when the multitude that attended him strewed palm-branches in his way.

Palm-tree,' in botany. See Phoenix.

Palma isle, one of the Canary-islands, sixty miles northwest of Teneriff.

palmaris.c: PALMARIS. in anatomy. See Anatomy, p. J99.

palmated.c: PALMATED, fomethingrefemblingthe (hapeof the hand : thus we say palmated leaves, roots, stones, he.

palmipedes.c:
PALMIPEDES, among ornithologists, the same with webfooted birds.

palmistry.c: PALMISTRY, a kind of divination, or rather a deceitful art pra<diied by gypsies, who pretend to foretell events by looking upon the lines and marks ol the hand.

palmyra.c: PALMYRA, the ruins of a magnificent city, in the province of Syria, two hundred miles south-ead of Aleppo.^

palos.c: PALOS, a port-town of Spain, situated on the bay of Cadiz : W. long. 70 15', N. lat. 370.

palpable.c: PALPABLE, something perceiveable by the senses, parti* cularly that of feeling.

palpitation.c:
PALPITATION, a spastic contraaion of the heart, when it se"ps and beats violently.

PAL.SY, in medicine. See Medicine, p. 97.

paludamentum.c:
PALUDAMENTUM, in Roman antiquity, a habit that differed in little' from the chlamys, except that this last belonged . chiefly to the lower class of people. See Chlamys.

PALUMEUS. See Columba.

paly.c:
PALY, or Palf/, in heraldry, is when the shield is divided into four or more equal parts, by perpendicular lines falling from the tep to the bottom. See Plate CXXXIV. fig. ic.

Paly bendy is when the escutcheon is divided by perpendicular lines, which is paly ; and also by diagonals, which is called bendy. See the article Bendy.

pampeluna.c: PAMPELUNA, the capital of Spanish Navarre, is the fee of a, bishop, and an university: W. long. i° 3c/, N. lat. 43° 15'.

panacea.c: PANACEA, among physicians, denotes an universal medicine, or a remedy for ail diseases ; a thing impossible to be obtained.

panada.c: PANADA, a diet confiding of bread boiled in water to the confidence of a pulp, and sweetened with a little sugar.

panama.c: PANAMA, the capital city of the province of Darien, in S.south America, where the treasures of gold and silver, and the other rich merchandize of Peru, are lodged in magazines till they are sent to Europe W. long. 82°, N. lat. 90.

panaro.c:
PANARO, a river of Italy, which rifing in the Appenine mountains, on the confines of Tuscany, divides Modena from Romania,, and then running through the Ferrarese falls into the Gulph of Venice.

PANATHENyEA, in Grecian antiquity, an ancient Athenian fedival, in honour of Minerva, who was the protectress of Athens, and called Athena.

panax.c: PAN AX, in botany, a genus of the polygamia dicecia class. The calix. of the hermaphrodite has five teeth, and the corolla five petals ; there are five stamina, and two fly li ; and the berry contains two feeds. The calix of the male is entire ; the corolla has five petals ; and there are five {lamina. The species are three, none of them natives of Britain.

panay.c: PANAY, the capital of the isle of Panay, one of the Philippine islands : E. long. 1190, and N. lat. 1 iQ.

pancarpus.c: PANCARPUS, in Roman antiquity, a kind of shew which the Roman emperors frequently exhibited to the people. In this spectacle, the circus being set all over with large trees, represented a fored, into which the beads being let from the dens under the ground; the people, at a sign given by the emperor, pursued, (hot, cut in pieces, and killed all they could lay hold of, which they afterwards carried away, to regale bpon at home. The beads usually given on these occasions were bears, deer, oxen, and sheep.

panchymagogue.c: PANCHYMAGOGUE, in pharmacy, a name given to some cathartic extracts. -

pancratium.c:
PANCRATIUM, among the ageients, a kind of exercise, which confided of wrest ling and boxing. In these contends it was cudomary for the weaker party, when he found himself pressed by his adversary, to fall down, and fight rolling on the ground.

Pancratium, in botany, a genus of the hexandria monogyma class. It has six petals, and a nedtarium divided into twelve segments, and the {lamina lie upon the nedtarium. There are Even species, none of them natives of Britain.

pandects.c: PAN DECTS, in the civil Jaw, collections made by Judinian’s order, of five hundred and thirty-four decisions of the ancient lawyers, on so many questions occurring in the civil law ; to which that emperor gave xhe force and authority of law, by an ep idle prefixed to thems The pandects consid of fifty books, and make the first part of the body of the civil law.

pandiculation.c: PANDICULATION, a dretching, ar that vio’ent and tensive motion of the solids, which usually accompanies the act of, yawning.

panegyric.c:
PANEGYRIC, an oration in praise of some extraordinary thing, person, or virtue.

Panegyrics' were anciently made in the public and fqlemn assemblies of the Greeks, either at their games, their feasts, or religious meetings.

panegyricum.c: PANEGYRICUM, in church-history, an ecclefiadical book, used by the Greek church, containing the panegyrical orations of various authors on the folerfmities of Jesus Christ and the faints.

pangonia.c: PANGONIA, in natural hide ry, the name of a genus of crystal, confiding of such as are composed of many angles.

panic.c: PANIC, denotes an ill-grounded terror or fright. /

panicle.c: PANICLE, in botany, denotes a fest woolly beard, on which the feeds of some plants, as millet, reeds, hang.

panicum.c: PANICUM, in botany, a genus of the triandria digynia class. The calix consids of three valves, the inmost cf which is lead. There are 28 species, four of which are natives of Britain, viz. the vi ride, or green panic-grafs ; the cruEgalli, or loose panic-grafs ; the sanguine se, or cock’s-foot panic-grafs ; and the dadlyion, or creeping panic grafs.

pannel.c:
PANNEL, inlaw, signifies the prisoner at the bar, or person who takes his trial before the court of judiciary, for some crime. See Law, Tit, xxxiii. 47.

Panness of a faddle , are two cushions or holders,- filled with cow’s, deer’s, or horse-hair,- and placed under the faddle, on each side, to prevent the bows and bands from galling the hors el

PANNICULUS Corn sour, in comparative anatomy, a robust fleshy tunic, situated in beads, between the tunic and the fat ; by means of which they can move their 1km in whole or part: it, is altogether wanting in mankind.

pantaloon.c: PANTALOON, a sort of garment, confiding of breeches and dockings all of one piece ; said to have been first introduced by the Venetians.

pantheon.c:
PANTHEON, in Roman antiquity, a temple of a circular form, dedicated to aii the gods : It was built by Agrippa, lon-indaw to Augudus; but is now converted into a church, and dedicated to the Virgin and all the martyrs.

PANTHER, in zoology. See Leo.

pantomime.c: PANTOMIME, a petson who imitates all' forts of a&sons and characters, by mere gedures, without speaking a word.

panuco.c: PANUCO, a city of Mexico, situated at the mouth of a river of the same name, and which falls into the gulph of Mexico : W. long. 103°, and N.lat. 230.

papaver.c: PAP AVER, in botany, a genus of the polyandria monogynia dafs. The corolla consists of four petals, and the calix of two se eyes. There are nine species, six of them natives of Britain, viz. the hybridum, or round roughheaded poppy ; the cambricum, or yellow poppy ; the somniferum, or wild poppy; the orgemone, or long rough-headed poppy ; the rhoeas, or red corn-poppy ; and the dubium, or long smooth-headed poppy. For the medical properties of poppy, see Opium.

paper.c:
PAPER, sheets of a thin matter, made of ibme vegetable fub dance. -

The materials on which mankind have, in different ages, contrived to write their sentiments, have been extremely various; in the early ages they made use of stones, and tables of wood, wax, ivory, <&c. See Book.

Paper, with regard to the manner~of making it, and the materials employed therein, is reducible to feveral kinds; as Egyptian paper, made of the rush papyrus; bark-paper, made of the inner rind of feveral trees ; cotton paper; incombudable paper; and European paper, made of linen rags.

Egyptian paper was principally used among the ancients; being made of the papyrus, or biblus, a species of rush which grew on the banks of the N !e In making it into paper, they began with lopping off the two extremes of the plant, the head * and the root ; the remaining part, which was the stem, they cut lengthwise into two nearly equal parts, and from each of these they Gripped the sca- ]y pellicles of which it confided. The innermost of these pellicles were looked on as the bed, and that neared the rind as the word : they were therefore kept apart, and made to con dilute two different forts of paper. As the pellicles were taken off, they extended them on a table, laying them over each other transversely, so as that the fibres made right angles : in this date they were glued together by the muddy waters of the Nile ; or, when tbose' were not to be had, with pade made of the fined wheat-flour, mixed, with hot water and a sprinkling cf vinegar. The pellicles were next pressed to get out the water, then dried, and laftly flatted and smo.othed by Lbating them with a mallet : this was the Egyptian paper, which was sometimes farther polished by rubbing it with a glass-ball, or the like.

Bark-pa ner was only the inner whitish rind, inclosed between the bark and the wood of feveral trees, as the maple, plane, beech,’ and elm, but especially the tilia, or linden-tree, which was that mossly used for this purpose.

On this dripped off, flatted, and dried, the ancients wrote books, feveral of which are said to be dill extant,

Chinese paper is of various kinds. Some is made of xthe rinds or banks of trees, especially the mulberry-tree and elm, but chiefly of the bambu and cotton-tree. la fa&, almost each province has its feveral paper. The preparations of paper made of the banks of trees, may be indanced in that of the bambu, which is a tree of the cane or reed kind. The second skin of the bark, which is soft and white, is ordinarily made use of for paper : this is beat in fair water to a pulp, which they take up in la^ge moulds, so that some sheets are above twelve feet ia length; they are completed, by dipping them sheet by sheet, in alum-water, which ferves indeed of the size among us, and not only hinders the paper from imbibing the ink, but makes it look as if varmihed over. This paper is white, soft, and close, without the lead roughness; though it cracks more easily than European paper, is very subject to be eaten by the worms, and its thinness piakes it liable to be soon worn out.

‘ Cottonpaper is a sort of paper which has been in use upwards of six hundred years. In the French king’s library are manuscripts on this paper, which appear to be of the Xth century ; and from the Xllth century, cotton manuscripts are more frequent than parchment ones. Cotton-paper is dill made in the Ead-Xndies, by beating cotton rags to a pulp.

Linen or European paper appears to have been first introduced among us towards the beginning of the XIVth century; but by whom this valuable commodity was invented, is not known. The method of making paper of linen or hempen-rags, is as follows. The linen-rags being carried to the mill, are first forted, then washed very clean in puncheons, whose fides are grated with |strong wires, and the bottoms bored full of holes. After this they are fermented, by laying them in heaps close covered with sacking, till they sweat and rot, which is commonly done in four or five days. When duly fermented, they are twist ed into handfuls, cut small, and thrown into oval mortars, made of well-seasoned oak, about half a yard deep, with an iron-plate at bottom, an inch thick, eight inches broad, and thirty long ; in the middle is a washing block, grooved, with five holes in it, and a piece of hair sieve fadened ontheinfide; this keeps' the hammers from touching it, and prevents any thing going our except the soul water. These mortars are coatinually supplied with water, by little troughs from a ciftenv fed by buckets fixed to the feveral floats of a great wheel, which raises the wooden hammersfor pounding the rags in the mortars. When the rags are beaten to a certain degree, called the first duff, the pulp is removed into boxes, mads like corn chan :* rs bi-ns, with the bottoni-board aflant/ and a little separation on the front for the water to drain away. The pulp of the rags being in; they take away as many of the front boards, as are needful, and prefs the mafs, hard down with their hands; the next day they pur on another board, and add more pulp, till the box is full; and here it remains mellowing a week, more or lefs, according to the weather. After this, the duff is again put into clean mortars, and is beaten afresh, and removed into boxes, as before, in which date it is called the second ftpff. The rrtafs is beat 'a third time, till some of it being mixed with fair water, and brewed to and fro*

ved, and is then carried to the vat, to be formed into sheets of paper. But lately, instead of pounding the rags to a pulp with large hammers, as above, they make ufeof an engine, which performs the work in much lefs time. This engine consists of a round solid piece of wood, into which are fattened feveral long pieces of tteel, ground very (harp. This is placed in a large trough with the rags, and a sufficient quantity of water. At the bottom of the trough is a plate with tteel bars, ground sharp like the former ; and the engine being carried round with prodigious velocity, reduces the rags to a pulp in a very short time. It mut be observed, that the motion of the engine caufes the water in the trough to circulate, and by that means constantly returns the fluff to the engine. The trough is conttantly fed with clean water at one end, while the dirty water from the rags is carried of at the other, through a hole, defended with wire gratings, in order to hinder the pulp from going out with the dirty water.

When the fluff is sufficiently prepared as above, it rs carried to the vat, and mixed with a proper quantity of water, which they call priming the vat. The vat is rightly primed, when the liquor has such a proportion of the pulp, as that the mould, on being dipped into it, will just take up enough to make a fleet of paper of the thickness required. The mould is a kmdsof sieve exactly of the size of the paper to be m&de, and about an inch deep, the bottom being formed of* fine brass wire, guarded underneath withfticks, to prevent it bagging down, and to keep it horizontal ; and further, to strengthen the bottom, there are large wires placed in parallel lines, at equal distances, which form those lines visible in all white paper when held up to the light : the mark of the paper is also made in this bottom, by interweaving a Jarge wire in any particular form. This mould the maker dips into the liquor, and gives it a {hake as he takes stout, to clear the water from the pulp. He then Aides it along a groove to the coucher, who turns out the (beet upon a felt laid on a plank, and lays another felt on it; and returns the mould to the maker, who by this time has prepared a second fleet in another mould : and thus they proceed, laying alternately a fleet and a felt, till they have made six quires of paper, which is called a post; and this they do, with such swiftness, that, in many forts of paper, two .men make twenty posss or more in a day. A pott of paper being made, either the maker jor coucher whittles ; on which four or five men advance, one of whom draws it under the prefs, and the ret prefs it with great force, till all the water is squeezed from it ; after w! ich it is separated fleet by fleet Som the felts, and laid regularly one fleet upon another; and having undergone a second pressing, it is hung up to dry. When fufficisntly dried, it is taken off the lines, rubbed smooth with the hands, and laid by till sized, which is the next operation. For this they chuse a fine temperate day ; and having boiled a proper quantity of clean parchment, or vellum shavings, in water, till it comes to a size, they prepare a fine cloth, on which they strew a due proportion of white vitriol and rock-alum finely powdered, and train the size through it into a large tub; in which they dip as much paper at once as they can conveniently

bear it. After this, the paper is pressed, hung up fleet by fleet to dry; and being taken down, is forted, and what is only fit for outside-quires laid by themselves* it is then told into quires, which are folded and pressed. The broken sheets are commonly put together, and two of the word quires* are placed on the outside of every ream or bundle ; and being tied up in wrappers, made of the fettling of the vat, it is fit for sale.

Paper is of various kinds, and used for various purposes : with regard to colour, it is principally dittinguiflied into white, blue, and brown; and with regard to its dimensions, dnto atlas, elephant, imperial, super-royal, royal, medium, demy, crown, foolscap, and pot-paper.

Paper-office, an office in the palace of Whitehall, in which all the public writings, matters ofttate and counci, proclamations, letters, intelligences, negotiations' abroad, and generally all difpaches that pass through the offices of the secretaries ofttate, are lodged, by way of library.

paphlagonia.c: PAPHLAGONIA, an ancient province of the letter Asia, situated on the Euxine-sea, now part of the province of Amalia in Turky.

paphos.c: PAPHOS, once an elegant city at the weft end of the island of Cyprus ; but the little town of Basso is now all that reniams of it.

papilio.c: PAPILIO, the butterfly, in zoology, a genus of infers belonging to the order of lepidoptera. It has four wings, imbricated with akindof downy feales ; the tongue is convoluted in a spiral form ; and the body is hairy. There are 273 species, principally distinguished by the colour of their wings.

papilionaceous.c: PAPILIONACEOUS, among botanists, an appellation’ given to the flowers of plants belonging principally to the diadelphia ciass, from their resembling the figure of a butterfly.

papous.c: PAPOUS, or New Guinea, a large continent in the Pacific ocean, a little south of the equator; situated east of the Spice islands, in 130° east long, but how far it extends farther to the eastward or southward, is uncertain.

pappus.c: PAPPUS, in botany, a soft downy substance, that grows on the feeds of certain plants, as thirties, hawkweed, &c. serving to scatter and buoy them up in the air.

par.c: PAR, in commerce, signifies any two things equal in value. See Commerce.

parable.c:
PARABLE, a fable, or allegorical instru&ion, founded on something real or apparent in nature or history, from which a moral is drawn, by comparing it with something in which the people are more immediately concerned; such are the parables of Dives and Lazarus, of the Prodigal Son, of the Ten Virgins, <bc.

PARABOLA. See Conic Sections.

paracentesis.c: PARACENTESIS, an operation in surgery, commonly called tapping. See Surgery.

paraclet.c: PARACLET, the Comforter, a name given to the Holy Ghott. _ *

paradisea.c:
PARADISEA, in ornithology, a genus belonging to the order of picae. The beak is covered with a belt or collar of downy feathers at the base ; and the feathers on the fides are very long. There are three species, viz. 1. The apoda, has the feathers on the fides longer than the body, and two long bristly feathers in the tail. It is the greater bird of paradise, and feeds upon butterflies. They

are Found in large flocks in the Molucca islands. 2. The regia, has two intermediate prime tail-feathers like threads and feathery at the points. It is found in Araboina. 3. The tristis, has a naked triangular spot behind the eyes; and the head and neck are of a dusky colour. It is a native of the Philippine isles, and feeds upon grafs-hoppers and other infedls.

paradise.c:
PARADISE, a term principally used for the gardens of Eden, in which Adam and Eve were placed immediately upon their creation.

As to this terrestrial paradise, there have been many inquiries about situation. It has been placed in the third heaven, in the orb of the moon, in the moon itself, in the middle region of the air, above the earth, under the earth, in the place possessed by the Caspian sea, and under the arctic pole. The learned Huetius places it upon the river that is produced by the conjunction of the Tigris and Euphrates, now called the river of the Arabs, between this conjunction and the division made by the same river before it falls into the Persian sea. Other geographers have placed it in Armenia, between the sources of the Tigris, the Euphrates, the Araxis, and the Phasis, which they suppose to be the four rivers described by Mofes.

The cele'Ctial paradise is that place of pure and refined delight, in which the souls of the blessed enjoy everlasting happiness.

Bird of Paradise. See Paradisea.

paradox.c:
PARADOX, in philosophy, a proposition feemingjy absurd, as being contrary to some received opinion, but yet true in faCt.

No science abounds more with paradoxes than geometry : thus, that a right line should continually approach to the hyperbola, and yet never reach it, is a true paradox ; and in the same manner, a spiral may continually approach to a point, and yet not reach it, in any number of revolutions, however great.

PARAEA, in zoology. See Coluber.

paragoge.c: PARAGOGE, in grammar, a figure whereby a letter or syllable is added to the end of a word ; as medt for me; dicier , for diciy See.

paraguay.c: PARAGUAY, or La Plata, a province of South America, subject to Spain, lies between 120 and 37° S. lat. and between 50° and ,75° W. long.

paralipomena.c: PARALIPOMENA, in matters of literature, denotes a supplement of things omitted in a preceding work.

parallactic.c: PARALLACTIC, in general, something relating to the parallax of heavenly bodies. See Parallax,

parallel.c:
PARALLEL, in geometry, an appellation given to lines, surfaces, and bodies every where equitiiflant from each other. See Geometry.

Parallels of latitude , in astronomy, are lesser circles of the fpliere parallel to the ecliptic, imagined to pass through every degree and minute of the colures.

Parallels of altitude , or almu.cantars, are circles parallel to the horizon, imagined to pass through every degree and minute of the meridian between the horizon and zenith, having their poles in the -zenith.

Parallels of declination , in agronomy, are the same with parallels of latitude in geography.

Parallel sphere, that situation of the sphere, wherein Vol. Ill, N° 88. .2

the equator coincides with the horizon, and the poles with the zenith and nadir.

Parallel sailing. See Navig at i on.

Parallelopiped, in geometry, a regular {olid comprehended under six parallelograms, the opposite ones whereof are similar, parallel, and equal.

parallelogram.c: PARALLELOGRAM, in geometry, a quadrilateral right lined figure, whose opposite fides are parallel and equal to each other.

parallelopipedia.c:
PARALLELOPIPEDIA, in natural history, the name of a genus of spars, thus called, because regularly of a paraiklopiped form.

They are pellucid crystalline spars externally of a determinate and regular figure, always found loose, detached, and separate from all other bodies, and in form of an oblique parallelopiped, with six parallelogram fides and ( eight solid angles, easily fissile either in an horrizontai or perpendicular direction, being composed of numbers of thin plates, and those of very elegantly and regularly arranged bodies, each of the same form with the whole mafs, except that they are thinner in proportion to their horizontal planes ; and naturally fall into these and no other figures, on being broken with a slight blow.

paralogism.c: PARALOGISM, in logic, a false reafomng, or a fault committed in demonstration, when a consequence is drawn from principles that are false, or, though true, are not proved ; or when a proposition is passed over that fliould have been proved by the way.

paramecia.c: PARAMECIA, in natural history, a name given to such animalcules as have no visible limbs or tails, and are of an irregularly oblong figure.

parameter.c: PARAMETER, in conic sections, aconflant line, otherwise called latus redlum See Conic Sections.

paramount.c: PARAMOUNT, in law, signifies the supreme lord of the fee.

paranymph.c: PARANYMPH, among the ancients, the person who waited on the bridegroom, and directed the nuptial solemnities ; called also pronubus, and aufpex, “because the ceremonies began by taking auspicia. As the paranymph officiated only on the part of the bridegroom, a woman called pronuba officiated on the part of the bride.

parapet.c:
PARAPET, in fortification, an elevation of earth designed for covering the soldiers from the enemies cannon or (mail (hot. See Fortification.

PARAPHERNAL goods in Scots law. See Law, Tit. vi. 8.

paraphimosis.c: PARAPHIMOSIS, in medicine, a disorder in the penis, wherein the prepuce is shrunk, and withdrawn behind the glans, so as not to be capable of being brought to cover the same ; which generally happens in venereal disorders. See Medicine.

paraphrase.c: PARAPHRASE, an explanation of some text, in clearer and more ample terms, whereby is supplied *what the author might have said or thought on the subjest ; such are esteemed Erasmus’s paraphrase on the New Teslament, the Chaldee paraphrase on the -Pentateuch, &c.

paraphrenitis.c: PARAPHRENITIS, in medicine, an inflammation of the diaphragm. See Medicine.

paraphrosyne.c:
PARAPHROSYNE, a word used by medical writers to express a delirium, or an alienation of mind in fevers, or from whatever cause.

parasite.c:
PARASITE, among the Greeks, was originally a very reputable title ; the parasites being a kind of priests, at lead ministers, of the gods, in the same manner as the Epulones were at R.ome. They took care of the sacred" corn, or the corn defined for theft service of the temples, and the gods, viz. sacrifices, feasts, <&c. they had even the intendance over sacrifices, and took care that they were duly performed. At Athens, there was a kind of college of twelve parafiteg ; each people of Attica furnishing one, who was always chosen out of the bell families.

. Polybius adds, that a parasite wa’s also an honourable,, title among the ancient' Gauls, and was given 'to their •poets ; but of late it has been made a term of reproach, and used for a flatterer and mean dependant.

parasites.c:
PARASITES, or parasitical plants, in botany,

. such plants as are produced out of the trunk or branches

*' of other plants, from whence they receive their nourishment, and will not grow upon the ground, as the misleto, fre.

Para state, in anatomy. See Anatomy, p.. 270.

parasynanche.c: PARAS YNANCHE, in medicine, a kind of angina, or quinsey See Medicine, p. 84.

pareuncle.c: PARE UNCLE, in a (hip, the name of a rope alrnalt like a pair of flings : it is feized both ends together, and then put double about any heavy thing thatjs to-be hoisted in or out of the Ihip ; having the hook of the runneri, hitched into it, to hoise it up by.

parcae.c: PAR CAE, in the heathen mythology, goddesses, who were supposed to preside over the accidents and events, and to determine the date or period, of human life. See Mythology.

parchment.c:
PARCHMENT, the'Ikins of Iheep or goats prepared after sucha manner as to render it proper for writing upon, covering books,

/The manufacture of parchment is begun by the Ikinner, and ftnifhed by the parchment-maker.

The skin having been Ilripped of its wool, and placed in the lime pit, the Ikinner Ilretches it on a kind of frame, and pares 6ff the fief ti withaniron instrument: this done, it is moistened with a rag ; and powdered chalk being spread over it, the Ikinner takes a large pumice-stone, flat at bottom, and rubs over the Ikin, and thus scow ers off the fief li: he then goes over it again with the iron instrument, moistens it as before, and rubs it again with the pumice-stone without any chalk underneath : this smooths and softens the flesh side very considerably. Fie then drains it again, by palling over it the iron instrument as before. The fief li-side "being thus drained, by scrap ing off the moisture, he in the same manner passes the iron over the wool or hair side: then Itretches it tight on a frame, andferapes the flesh side again : this finishes its draining ; and the more it is drained, the whiter it becomes. The Ikinner now throws on more chalk, sweeping it over with a piece of lamb Ikin that has the wool on; and this smooths it Hill farther. It is now left to dry; and when dried, taken off the frame, by cutting it

alf round The Ikin, thus far prepared' by the Ikin net, is taken out of his hands by the parchment-maker ; who first, awhile it is dry, parqs it on a summer (which is a calfikin Aretched in a frame) with a '{harper inilruraent than that used by the skinner, and, working with the arm from the top to the bottom of the Ikin, takes away about one half of its thickness. The Ikin, thus equally pared on ,the fief ii-side, is agaha rendered smooth, by being rubbed with the pumice-stone on a bench covered with a sack Huffed with flocks, which leaves the parchment in a condition fit for writing upon. The parings thus taken off the leather, are used in making glue, size, <&c.

What is called vellum, is only parchment made of the fk’ns of abortives, or at least sucking calves. This has a much finer grain, and is whiter and smoother than parchment ; but is prepared in the same manner, except its not being passed through the lime-pit.

PARDALUS. See Leo.

PAREGORICS in pharmacy, medicines that asswage pain, otherwise called anodynes.

PAREIRA brava, in the materia medics, a kind of oblong and large root, brought from the Brasils.

It is certainly a diuretic of no mean character, and has done great service in nephritic cafes; and in pleurisy es and quinseys it has been attended with more success than almost any medicine we know offingly.

parelcon.c: PARELCON, in grammar, a figure by which a word or syllable is added to theend of another.

parembole.c: PAREMBOLE, in rhetoric, a figure wherein something relating to the subjest is inserted in the middle of a period. All the differences between the parembole and parenthesis, according to Vossius, is, that the former relates to the subjest in hand, whereas the latter is foreign to it.

parenchyma.c:
PARENCHYMA, in anatomy, a term introduced by Erafiflratus, signifying all that substance which is contained in the interlaces betwixt the blood -v^ffels of the viscera, which he imagined to be extravafiued and concreted blood.

Parenchyma of plants . Grew applies the term parenchyma to the pith or pulp, or that inner part of a fruit or plant through which the juice is supposed to be distributed. See Agriculture.

parent.c: PARENT, a term of relation applicable to those from whom we immediately receive our being.

parentalia.c: PARENTALIA, in antiquity, funeral obfequics, or the last duties paid by children to their deceased parents.

parenthesis.c: PARENTHESIS, in grammar, certain intercalary words, inserted in a discourse, which interrupt the sense, or thread, but seem necessary for the better understanding of the subjest.

parenzo.c: PARENZO, orPiRENZo, a porttown of IAria, in the territory of Venice, situated _on a bay of the gulpIYof Venice, twenty five miles south of Cabo de IAria,

paresis.c:
PARESIS, in medicine, is defined to be a palsy of the bladder, wherein the mine is either suppressed, or discharged involuntarily.

PAPvETONIUM, in natural history, the name of an earth anciently found on the Ihores of Egypt, Cyrene, and the island of Crete, and used by the ancients in pairing.

parget.c: PARGET, in natural history, a name given to feveral kinds of gypsum, or plaster-stone.

pargeting.c:
PARGETING, in building, is used for the plastering of walls, and sometimes for plaster itself.

P ARHELIUM , or Par hem on, in phy-fief ogy, a mock lun, or rue tear, in form of a very bi sight light, appearing cn one side of the sun.

The parhelia are formed by the reflexion of the sun’s beams on a cloud properly posited. They usu&lly accompany the ccronce, or luminous circles, and are placed in the same circumference and. at the same height. Their colours resemble that of the rain boy/, the red and yellow are on the side towards the sun, and the blue and violet on the other. There are corones sometimes seen without parhelia, and vice verja.

Parhelia are double, triple, &c, and in 1629 a Par~ he lion of five funs was seen at Rome, and in i666'another at Arles of six,

M. Muriotte accounts for parhelia from an inanity of little particles of ice floating in the air, that multiply the image of the sun by refraction or -reflection ; and by a geometrical calculus he has determined the precise figure of these little icicles, their situation in the air, and the size of the coronae of circles which accompany the parhelia, and the colours wherewith they are painted.

paria.c:
PARIA, a lake ofPeru, in South America, in the province of Los Charcas, situated in 67° W. long, and 22 0 S. lat.

PARIETALIA ossa, in anatomy. See Anatomy, p.

parietaria.c: PARIETARIA, in botany, a genus of the polygamia moncecia giass. The calix, both in the female and hermaphrodite, consist is of four segments ; none of them have any corolla ; the hermaphrodite has four stamina; and both have one stylus, and ore long feed. There are six species, only one of them, viz. the officinalis, or pellitory of the wall, is a native of Britain. It is esteemed a** cooling and abstergent.

paris.c:
PARIS, in botany, a genus of the oClandria trigynia class. The calix consists of four leaves, and the-corolla of four narrow petals ; and the berry has four cells. There is but one species, vis. the quadrifolia, herb-paris, or truelove, a native of Britain.

Paris, in geography, the metropolis of the kingdom of France, and of the principality or government of the isle of France, situated in E. long. 2° 2$', N. lat 48° 50’, two hundred miles south-east of London, six hundred and eighty north-eafit of Madrid, five hundred and fifty weft of Vienna, one thou land three hundred north-weft of Constantinople, and seven hundred north-weft of Rome.

parish.c: PARISH, the precinct of a parochial church, or a circuit of ground inhabited by people who belong to one church and are under the particular charge of its minister.

park.c: PARK, a large indo sure privileged for wild beasts of chace, either by prefcriptioii or the king’s grant.

parkinsonia.c: PARKINSONIA, in botany, a genus of the decandria monogynia class. The calix consists of four segments, and the corolla of four oval petals, the lowest being kidney shaped ; it has no stylus ; and the pod is cylindrical.

parley.c: PARLEY, a conference with an enemy. Hence to beat or found .a parley, is to give a signal for held ing such a conference by beat of drum or found of trumpet,

parliament.c:
PARLIAMENT, is the grand assembly of the three states of this .kingdom, fummqped together, by the king’s authority, to consult or matters relating to the public welfare, and particularly to ena<st and repeal laws. It consists of the king, the lords spiritual. and temporal, aod

the commons,, and is at once the st at of t!*t Lgift'.live authority, and the highest court of justice in Great-Sir rain. In the house of lords, criminal caufts are tried on the impeachment of the commons ; and this house has an original jurif'didiion for the trial of peers upon indictments found by a grand jury-, the lords likewise try such civ-fes as come thither on appeals from the court c-f chancery, and all their decrees are as judgments. The house of commons examine the right of elections ; regulate di.spates concerning them ; may expel their own members, and * commit them to prison. They are the grand inquest of the nation ; and present public grievances or delinquents to the king and lords, in order to their being punished. In sliort, they are the representatives of a.li the commons in the kingdom; and in them their constituents have placed the highest confidence, by inverting them with the power of making laws, and entrusting them with all their liberties and privileges.

Originally, new parliaments were called every year - but by degrees their term grew longer. In the reign of king Charles II. they were held a long time, with great interruptions between ; but both methods were found of such ill consequence, that, in the beginning of the reign of king William III. an aft was passed, by which the term of all parliaments was restrained to three sessions, or three years ; this was hence called the trienni.il aft : but fines that time, from other views, the period of parliaments has been lengthened to seven years. A parliament is called by the king’s writ or letter directed to each lord, commanding him to appear; and by other writs, directed to the sheriffs of each county, to summon the%peop!e to eleft two knights for each county, and one or two burgesses for each borough. The number of the members in the house of lords is uncertain, as increasing at the king’s pleasure. ''The members of the house of commons, when full, are five hundred and fifty-three ; viz. ninety two knights of the {hires ; fifty two deputies for twentyfive cities, London having four ; sixteen for the eight cinque-ports; two for each university; three hundted and thirty two for an hundred and eighty boroughs ; twelve for the boroughs in Wales, and forty-five members for Scotland. If three hundred of these members are met, it is reckoned a full house ; and forty may compose a house for the dispatch of business.

Upon the holding of a parliament, the king, the first day, fits in the upper-house, under a canopy, with the crown on his head, and drafted in his royal robes; and there, by himself, or the lord chancellor, declares the - reasons of their meeting, in the presence of both the lords and commons ; and then the commons are required to chuse a speaker, who is presented to the king, and being approved by his majesty,. the business of the parliament goes on.

The lords and commons fit each in a distin-Ct apartment : in the house of lords, the princes of the blood fit by themselves on the fides £>f the throne ; at the wall, on the king's right hand, the two archbiftiops fit by themselves on a form. Below them, the bishops of London, Durham, and Winchester* and all the other bishops, fit according to the priority of their consecration. On the king’s left hand the lord-treasurer, lord prefident, and lord privy-feal, fit upon forms above all dukes, except the royal bleed ; then the dukes, marquiftes, and earls, according,;

A-cross the room are woolsacks, continued from an ancient custom ; and the chan cellor, or keeper, being of co.urse the speaker of the house ;of lords, fits on the first wool-sack before the throne, with the great seah or mace lying by him; below these are forms for the viscounts and barons. On the of tier woolsacks are feated the judges, makers in chancery, and king’s council, who are only to give their advice in points of lav/: but they all (land up till the king gives them leave to fit. The commons fit promiscuously ; only the speaker has a chair at the upper end of the house, and the clerk and his assistant fit at a table near-him. Before any business is done, all the members of the house of commons take the oaths of allegiance and supremacy^ &c. and subscribe their opinions against transubstantiation, &c. and if any member of that house votes, or fits there during any debate, arter the speaker is chosen, without having first taken these oaths, between the hours of nine and four, in a full house, he is adjudged a Popish recusant convict, and incapable of any office, and forfeits five hundred pounds. The same test the lords too, though they do not take the oaths, are obliged to comply with. When the parliament is thus met, no members are to depart from it without leave. Upon extraordinary occasions, all the members are sometimes summoned ; in which cafe every lord spiritual and temporal, and every knight, citizen, and burgess, is to come to parliament, except he can reasonably and honestly excuse himfejf ; or be amerced ; that is, respectively, a lord by the lords, and a commoner by the commons.

Ail members of parliament, in order that they may atl arid the public service of their country, have the privilege for themfdves of being free from arrests, attach-* ments, imprisonment/ for debts, trespasses, &c.

but not from arrests for treason, felony, and breach of the peace.

As to thede&ionof members, it is ena&ed, That candidates (hall not make any presents of money to, or treat the electors, after the test of the writ of the summons, or the if tiling out of the writs for elections, or after any seat for a member of parliament is become vacant ; in cafe they do, tbev are declared incapable of serving as members, by 7 W, III. c. 4. And farther, an oath is to be taken by ele&ors, That they have not either received, or had any money, gift, reward, orany office, place, employment, or even promise of money, gift, <bc . to them or their use, to give their votes ; and in these cafes, if they ask, take, or contra# for money or reward, either by gift or other device, to give or refuse their votes for any one.; or if persons, by gift, <&c, corruptly procure any ele#or to give his vote; they (hall forfeit five hundred pounds, and be totally disabled to vote at any election of members of parliament, as also to hold' any office, franchise, <&c. Likewise officers who admit persons to vote without their taking the aforementioned scath, in cafe the same be demanded, incur a forfeiture of one hundred pounds ; and an oath is to be adminiftred to all the returning officers, that they have not received any money, gift, or place, for the making of their returns : 2 Geo. II. c. 24. 9 Geo. II, c. 38. A knight of the ihire must be worth six hundred pounds a- «year in land, and all other members three hundred pounds,.

Anciently all the people had votes in elections, till It was ena&ed by Henry VI. that none but freeholders, who had a yearly revenue of forty (hillings, ffiould be admitted to vote for knights of the (hire.

The manner of debating upon, and passing bills in parliament, is as follows: Any member may move, to have a bill brought in, which, upon a question put, being agreed to by the majority, this person, with others, is ordered to prepare and bring in the same. When it is ready, a time is appointed for its being r^ad; and after the clerk’s reading it, the speaker reads an abftra# of it, and puts the question whether or no it (hall have a second reading ; and after a second reading, the question is put whether or no it (hall be committed, which is either to a ccmmitee of the whole house if it be of importance, or to a private comm.tee, any member naming the persons. The committee being appointed, and a'chairman chosen, the chairman reads the bill paragraph by paragraph, puts every clause to the question, fills up the blanks, and makes amendments, according to the opinion of the majority. The bill thus gone through, the chair-man makes his report at the side-bar of the house, reads all the additions and amendments, &c. and moves for leave to bring up the report to the table ; which granted, he delivers it to the clerk, who reads the amendments, The speaker then puts the question whether they (hall be read a second time; and if agreed to, he reads them himself. To so many of the amendments as the house acquiesces in, the question is now put, Whether the bill, thus amended, shall be ing rosied and written fair upon parchment, and read a third time? and the bill being ing rosied, the speaker holds it in his hand, and asks if it shall pass. If the majority be for it, the clerk writes on it, Soit bailie aux fs'tgneursy “ Let it be delivered to the lords or if in the house of lords, Soit bailie aux communes* “Letit be delivered to the commons.” If a bill berejefted, it cannot be any more proposed during that session. A bill for a general pardon has but one reading.

When a member of the house of commons speaks, he /lands up uncovered, and directs his speech to the speaker only. If what he fays be answered by another, he is not allowed to reply the same day, unless personal reflections have been cast upon him : but when the commons, in order to have a greater freedom of debate, have resolved themselves into a comittee of the whole house, every member may /peak to a question as often as he thinks neceftary. In the house of lords they vote, beginning at the puisne, or lowed baron and so up orderly to the highest, everyone answering Content or Not content . In the house of commons they vote by yeas and rays ; and if it be dubious which are the greater number,' the house divides. If the question be about bringing any thing into the house, the yeas go out ; but if it be about any thing the house already has, the rays go out. In all divisions the speaker appoints four tellers, two of each opinion. In a committee of the whole house, they divide by changing fides, th q yeas taking the right and the rays the left of the chair ; and then there are but two tellers. If a bill pass one house, and the other demur to it, a conference is demanded in the painted chamber, where certain members are deputed from each house; and here the lords fit covered, and the commons stand bare and debate the cafe. If they disagree, the affair is null ; but if they a-'

Parliaments of France, are sovereign courts, eftabliflied by the king, finally to determine all disputes between particular persons, and to pronounce on appeals from Sentences given by inferior judges. There are ten of these parliaments in france, of which that of Paris is the chief, its privileges and juris di&ion being of the greatest extent. Jt consists of six chambers," viz. the grand chamber, where caufes of audience are pleaded; and five chambers of inquest, where procettes are adjudged in writing. This parliament enjoys the privileges ot verifying anderegiftring the king’s arrets or edi&s, without which those edi&s are of little or no value.

Parliament of Sweden, consists of four estates, with the king at their head: These states are, i . The nobility and representatives of the gentry; with whom the colonels, lieutenant-colonels* majors, and captains of every regiment, fit and vote. 2. The clergy; one of which body is elected from every rural deanery of ten parishes ; who, with the bishops and superintendents, amount to about two hundred. 3 . The burghers, elected by the magistrates and council of every corporation as their representatives, of whom there are four for Stockholm, and two for every other town, amounting in the whole to about an hundred and fifty. 4. The peasants, chosen by the peasants out of every district ; who chuse one of their own rank, and not a gentleman, to represent them: these amount to about two hundred and fifty.

All these generally meet at Stockholm ; and after the state-afFairs have been represented to them from the throne, they separate, and fit in four feveral chambers or houses, in each of which affairs are carried on by majority of votes; and every chamber has a negative in the palling any law.

PARTI, Partie, Party, or Parted, in heraldry, is applied to a shield or escutcheon, denoting it divided or marked out into partitions.

Parti per fefs is when the cut is across the middle, from side to side.

Par ti per bend dexter, is when the cut corned from the upper corner of the Ihield, on the right hand, and defeends athwart to the opposite lower corner.

Parti per bend sinister, is when the cut, coming from the upper left corner, defeends across to the opposite lower one.

From these four partitions have proceeded an infinite number of others, of various and extravagant forms.

It is the various arrangement and texture of these partidas, with the difference of cohesion, &c. that constitute the various kinds of bodies. The smallest particles cohere with the strongest attradion, and compose bigger particles of weaker cohesion; and many of these cohering compose bigger particles, whose vigour is still weaker ; and hereupon the operations in chemistry, and the colours of natural bodies, depend, and which, by cohering, compose bodies cf sensible bulk. The cohesion of the particles of matter, the Epicureans imagined, was esse ded by means of hooked atoms; the Aristotelians, by reft; but Sir Isaac Newton shews, that it is done by means of a certain power, whereby the particles mutually atl rad and tend towards each other. By this attradionof the particles, he shews, that most of the phenomena of the left er bodies are afleded, as those of the heavenly bodies are, by the attradion of gravity.

pasquin.c: PASQUIN, a mutilated ftatub at Rome, in a corner of the palace of the Ursini : it takes its name from a cobler of that city called Pasquin, famous for his sneers and gibes, and who diverted himself with palling his jokes on all the people who went through that street. After his death, as they were digging up the pavement before his shop, they found in the earth the statue of an ancient gladiator, well cut, but maimed, and half spoiled : this they set up in the place where it was found, and by common consent named it Pasquin. Since that time, all satires are attributed to that figure ; and are either put into its mouth, or pasted upon it, as if they were wrote by Pasquin redivivus ; and these are addressed by Pasquin to Marforio, another statue at Rome. When Marforio is attacked, Pasquin comes to his assistance ; and when Pasquin is attacked, Marforio assists him in his turn.

Among the birds of passage, the fieldfare, the redwing, the woodcock, and the snipe, come to us ia the autumn, at the time when the

summer-birds are leaving us, and go from n« again in spring, at the time when these return ; and of these the two last often continue with us through the summer, and breed ; so that the two first seem the only kinds that certainly leave us at the approach of spring, retiring to the northern parts of the continent, where they live during the summer, and breed ; and at the return of winter, are driven southerly from those frigid climes, in search of food, which there the ice and snow must deprive them of.

passions.c:
PASSIONS, in moral philosophy, are certain motions of the soul, which make it pursue what appears to be good, arid avoid whatever threatens evil.

By reflecting, fays Mr Locke, on the various modifications or tempers of the mind, and the internal sensations which pleasure and pain, good and evil, produce in us, we may thence form to ourselves the ideas of our passions. Thus, by reflecting upon the thought we have of the delight which any thing is apt to produce in us, we form an idea which we call love. Defire is that uneasiness which a man finds in himself upon the absence-of any thing, the present enjoyment of which caufes delight.. Joy is a delight of the mind, a ising from the present, or assured approaching, pofRflion of fotne good. Sorrow is, an uneasiness of the mind, upon the thought of a good loft, or the sense of a present evil. Hope is a pleasure in the mind, upon th£ thought of a probable future enjoyment of a thing which is apt to delight. Fear is an uneasiness of the mind, upon the thought of a future evil likely to befall us Anger is a difeompofure of the mind, upon the receipt of injury, with a present purpose of revenge. Despair is the thought of the unattainableness of any good. Envy is an uneasiness of mind, caufed by the consideration of a good we defire, obtained by one we. think ftiould not have had it before us.

On the just regulation and subordination of the passions^ depends, in a great measure, the happiness of mankind.' See Moral Philosophy.

In the two first, the spirits are hurried with too great vivacity; whereas, in fear or dread, they are is it were curbed and concentrated : whence we may conclude, that they have a very' bad effeft upon health ;f and therefore it will be bed to keep them within bounds as much as polity se, and to preserve an inward serenity, calmness, and tranquillity.

Passions, in painting, are the external expressions of the different dispositions and affections of the mind': but parv ticularly their different effects upon the feveral features of the face : for though the arms, and indeed every part, of the body, serve likewise, by their quick, languid, and variously diversified motions, to express the passions of the soul ; yet, in painting, this difference is most; conspicuous in the face.

In sorrow, joy, love, st same, and compact fieri, the eyes swell all of a sudden, are covered with a superabundant moisture, and drop tears ; and in grief especially, the corners of the mouth hang down, the eye-lids are half flint, and the pupil of the eye is elevated and half covered ; and all the other musci es of the face are relaxed, so that the visage appears longer than ordinary.

♦ In fear, terror, fright, and horror, she eye-brows are greatly elevated ; the eye lids are expanded as wide as possible, so as to discover the white of the eye ; and the pupil is depressed, and half covered by the lower eye-lid; the hair stands an end ; the mouth is at the same time wide open ; and the lips so far drawn back, that the teeth both of the upper and under jaw appear.

Contempt is expressed by raising one side of the upper lip, so as to discover the teeth, whilst the other side has a movement like that in laughter ; the eye, on that side where the teeth appear, is half flint, whilst the other remains open ; however, both the pupils are depressed.

In jealousy, envy, hatred, and malice, the eye brows are knit *f and, in laughter, all the parts agree, tending as it were towards the centre of the face.

pastoral.c:
PASTORAL, in general, something that relates to ftiepherds; hence we say, pastoral life, manners, poetry, <&cj

The original of poetry is ascribed to that age which succeeded the creation of the world : and as the keeping of flocks seems to have been the first employment of mankind, the most ancient sort of poetry was, probably, pastoral. It is natural to imagine, that the leisure of tho fer ancient shepherds admitting and inviting foiqe diversion, none was so proper to that solitary and sedentary life as singing ; and that in their fongs they took occasion to celebrate their own felicity. From hence a poem was invented, and afterwards improved to a perfe<st image ofr that happy time ; which, by, giving us an esteem for the virtues of a. former -age, might recommend them to the present. And since the life of fliepherds was attended with more tranquillity than any other rural employment, the poets chose to introduce their persons, from whom it received the.name of Pastoral.

A pastoral is an imitation of the ad lion of a ftiepherd, or one considered under that character. The form of this; imitation is 'dramatic, or narrative, or mixed with both ; the fable Ample ; the manners not too polite, nor too ruftic ; the thoughts are plain, yet admit a little^ quickness and passion, but that sliort and flowing ; the expression humble, yet as pure as the language will afford;! neat, but not florid ; easy,. and yet lively.- In sliort, the fable, manners, thoughts, and expressions, are full of the greatest fimplicit^ in nature.

The complete character of this poem consists in simpli^- sity, brevity, and delicacy ; the two first of which render an eclogue natural, and the. last delightful

pearl.c:
PEARL, in natural history, a hard, white, shining body, usually roundifli, found in a tedaceous fish refenrbling an oyster. ■ - 9

Pearls, though esteemed of the number of gems by our j.v/ellers, and highly valued, not only at this time,' but in all ages, proceed only from a did semper in the creature that produces them, analogous to the bez.oars, and other felony concretions in feveral 2nim als of other kinds.

The fish in which these are. usually produced is the Eafl-Indian pearl-oyster, as it is commonly called Besides this {hell, there are many others that are found to produce pearls ; as the common oyster, the muscle, and feveral others ; the pearls of which are often very good but those of the true Indian berberi, or pearl-oyster, are in general superior to all. The small or feed-pearls, also called ounce-pearls, from their being sold by the ounce, and not by tale, are vastly the moll numerous and common ; but as in diamonds, among the multitudes or small ones, there are smaller numbers of larger found, so in pearls there are larger and larger kinds; but as they increase in size, they are proportionably lefs frequent, and this is one reason of their great price. We have Scotch pearls frequently as big as a little tare, some as big as a large pea, and some few of the size of a horse-bean ; but these are usually of a bad shape, and of little value in proportion to their weight. Philip II. of Spain had a pearl perfect in its shape and colour, and of the size of a pigeon’s pgg. The fined, and what is called the true fhspe of rhe pearl, is a perftft round ; but if pearls of a confiderable size are of the shape of a pear, as is not unfrequently the cafe, they are not lefs valued, as they serve for ear-rings and other ornaments. Their colour ought to be a .pure white, and that not a dead and lifeless, but a clear and' brilliant one ; they mud be perfe&ly free from any foulness, spot or datn ; and their surfaces mud be naturally smooth and glossy. for they bring their natural polish with them, which art is not able to improve

All pearls are formed of the matter of the {hell, and consid of a number of coats spread with perfefl regularity one over another, in the manner of the feveral coats of an onion, or like the feveral drata of the stones. found in the bladders or stomachs of animals, only muclr thinner.

Manner cf fish tug for Pearls in the East indies. There .are two seasons for pearl-fifhmg : the first is in March and 6 A Aprils
